plan: This ascending clock auction with sealed exit bids functions as a second-price auction: I win if my bid is highest, and I pay the second-highest bid, not my own. Therefore, bidding my true value ($25) is the dominant strategy—it maximizes expected profit since I only pay less than my bid when I win, and bidding higher or lower than true value only risks either overpaying or losing profitable opportunities. No history exists to suggest otherwise.

Since this is effectively a second-price auction (the winner pays the highest losing bid), the dominant strategy is to bid exactly my true value. Bidding my value ensures I win whenever it's profitable to do so (when my value exceeds others' bids) and never pay more than my value if I win. Bidding higher risks paying more than my value; bidding lower risks losing profitable opportunities. Therefore, I will bid $18, my true value.

Since the auction functions as a second-price auction (the winner pays the second-highest bid/exit price), the dominant strategy is to bid my true value. Bidding higher risks paying more than the item is worth to me if I win, while bidding lower risks losing an auction I could have profitably won. With a value of $31, bidding exactly $31 ensures I maximize expected profit: I win whenever the highest competing bid is below $31, paying only that competing bid, and I never overpay.
